consensus_summary: Light primarily symbolizes God’s own nature, holiness, truth, presence, and glory, fulfilled in Christ as the light of the world who brings revelation and salvation, always opposed to darkness; secondary but common senses include the word/law as guidance, moral purity, and believers’ reflective witness.
book_summary: Light is the law lived visibly as an example—obedient actions others can see (opposite: darkness).
consensus_core_identification: God’s nature/presence/truth and Christ as the divine light
book_core_identification: the law lived out visibly in obedient actions that serve as an example
boundary_disagreement: Consensus centers the divine/Christological referent and treats law, good works, and witness as derivative; the book centers only the visible human embodiment of the law and does not identify light with God or Christ.
material_contradiction: The consensus primary claim (God/Christ is light) and the book’s claim (visible law-obedience is light) assign incompatible primary referents to the same symbol in the same sense; accepting the book’s identification replaces rather than merely narrows the consensus core.
rationale: Minimum cores differ in referent: every consensus response fixes the primary meaning on God/Christ as light (1 Jn 1:5, Jn 8:12, Jn 1, etc.), while the book equates light solely with the law made visible in good works. Although Prov 6:23 and Matt 5:16 appear among consensus alternatives, they are secondary and derivative; elevating their fusion to the sole entry-level identification rejects the theocentric core. Hence the relation is divergent (replaced referent), not a refinement of boundaries around the same core, and not novel because the components are already listed as common alternatives.
strongest_objection: The reading ignores the dominant, cross-traditional identification of light with God and Christ themselves, reducing a theocentric symbol to one secondary ethical application.
